findings.evidence: scan() selects `files = tracked_files(root) if is_git_repo(root) else walked_files(root)`, and the CI step (`run: python3 tools/check_genericization.py`) executes inside an actions/checkout work tree, so production always takes the git-tracked branch. Yet the suite docstring says each case runs in a `temp tree, non-git -> the tree-walk branch`, and the only case touching the git branch, test_real_repo_root_is_clean, asserts merely rc 0 plus `genericization: 0 hit(s) in 0 file(s)` - which an empty scan satisfies; test_root_flag_honored_and_validated's default-root leg asserts only `assertNotIn("leak.md", proc.stdout)` with no rc or hit check. Named defeating change: stub `tracked_files` to `return []` (leave is_git_repo intact); every test in tools/tests/test_genericization_check.py stays green while the CI tripwire permanently prints `0 hit(s) in 0 file(s)`, exits 0, and waves banned-token leaks through.
findings.required_change: add a suite case that exercises the git branch as a detector: git-init a temp repo, commit a file containing a seeded token, run the tool with --root at it, and assert rc 1 plus the exact HIT line, so an empty or stubbed tracked-file enumeration fails the suite

findings.evidence: the new guard in check_bare_runners (`declared = contract.get("verify_commands")` / non-list -> `fail(...)`) sits after the early return `no runner names declared (--runner) - bare-invocation check inactive`. No test in the package reaches it: the unit assertion calls only `M.check_verify_commands({"verify_commands": 42}, ...)`, and the CLI case test_verify_commands_non_list_named passes no --runner, so check_bare_runners returns inactive before the guard runs. Deleting this guard leaves the whole suite green, while a production contract with declared runners and `verify_commands: 42` regresses to the raw TypeError the hunk's own comment (`named refusal, never TypeError (S2-F2)`) says must never happen.
findings.required_change: add a unit case calling check_bare_runners with a non-empty runners list and a non-list verify_commands, asserting the named `must be a list, got int` finding and no exception

findings.evidence: the normalization loop rewrites five keys (`files`, `tests`, `verify_commands`, `invariants`, `decisions`) to `[]` when non-list, justified by the comment `a list-typed field that failed the type check above already carries a NAMED finding`. The package proves that claim for only two of the five keys (the tests assert named findings for `files: 42` and `verify_commands: 42`); for `tests`, `invariants`, and `decisions` no test shows a named finding exists, and validate_contract's body is not in the package. If any of those three keys lacks a type finding upstream, the silent `[]` normalization makes downstream checks (tests coverage, invariants, decisions) pass vacuously with zero findings - and removing validate_contract's type check for one of those keys, or extending the normalization list to a key that never had one, leaves the suite green.
findings.required_change: add gate cases feeding non-list `tests`, `invariants`, and `decisions` through the plan/build CLI, each asserting a NAMED finding is emitted alongside the normalization, so the comment's claim is test-pinned for all five keys

findings.evidence: build_mode's new try/except around `diff_file.read_text` (named `manifest-diff` finding, `named refusal, never a raw traceback (S2-F2)`) is unreachable through the CLI: main() now pre-reads `args.diff_file` and returns rc 2 (`usage: unreadable ...`) before build_mode is ever called, and the only test for a bad diff file, test_missing_diff_file_is_usage_refusal, exercises just that pre-check. No test calls build_mode directly with an unreadable injected diff. Reverting the guard to a bare `diff_file.read_text(...)` - or deleting it - leaves the entire suite green while any programmatic caller (test harnesses, future embedders importing the module) regresses to a raw traceback on a non-UTF-8 diff.
findings.required_change: add a unit test that calls Gate.build_mode directly with a non-UTF-8 or unreadable --diff-file path and asserts the named `manifest-diff ... unreadable` finding with no traceback, so the guard is proven independent of the CLI pre-check

findings.evidence: _read_injected_json uses None as its failure sentinel and returns `json.loads(text)` on success; a --command-result or --ui-results file whose entire content is the valid JSON literal `null` therefore returns None indistinguishably from a read failure, and callers do `if parsed is None: return 2` - an rc-2 exit with NO `usage: unreadable ...` line printed, contradicting the helper's own contract (`Returns the parsed value, or None after printing usage: unreadable <path>`) and the S2-F2 named-refusal rule. No test covers a null-content evidence file, so the silent unnamed refusal ships green.
findings.required_change: separate the failure signal from parsed values (sentinel object or (ok, value) tuple) so valid JSON `null` is handled explicitly - either accepted as a legal empty evidence value or refused with the named usage line - and add a test pinning the chosen behavior

findings.evidence: the installed ignore template carries the patterns `*secret*` (line 6) and `*token*` (line 7) while ONBOARDING.md's apply list installs `factory/SECRETS.md` and `.gitignore` into the same target repo. On case-insensitive filesystems (macOS/Windows checkouts, where git sets core.ignorecase and matches ignore patterns case-insensitively) `*secret*` matches `factory/SECRETS.md`, so apply installs the secrets-posture doc but git silently never tracks it - an unhandled partial-install failure mode; the diff ships no check that every file apply installs survives the .gitignore it installs, and Linux CI (case-sensitive) can never catch it.
findings.required_change: narrow the pattern or add a negation (e.g. `!factory/SECRETS.md`) so installed template files are never ignored by the installed .gitignore, and add a verify/apply check (exercised case-insensitively) that no installed file matches the ignore rules

findings.evidence: carve-out 1 is implemented as a whole-line test - `if name == "agentmerlin" and "ai-software-factory" in line.lower(): continue` - while its documented intent is narrow: `clone URLs like github.com/agentmerlin8-ops/ai-software-factory pass`. Any agentmerlin occurrence on a line that merely mentions the factory name is carved out, so a leaking reference (e.g. `vendored from agentmerlin/[redacted]-ingest into ai-software-factory`) passes the tripwire; the guard is wider than the claim. test_agentmerlin_with_factory_identity_passes pins only the pass direction (a genuine clone URL), and no test distinguishes URL-shaped identity lines from arbitrary co-mentioned lines, so widening or keeping the broad form stays green either way.
findings.required_change: narrow the carve-out to the claimed shape (agentmerlin appearing as part of an ai-software-factory repo URL/host path on the line) and add a failing-case test for a bare agentmerlin reference that merely co-occurs with the factory name

findings.evidence: The shipped gitignore template ignores '*token*' (line 7) and '*secret*' (line 6) by bare substring: '+*secret*' / '+*token*'. apply installs this template into every onboarded control home (ONBOARDING.md: "- `factory/KICKOFF.md`, `factory/SECRETS.md`, `.gitignore`"). The patterns match ANY path containing the substring, not just secret stores — e.g. src/tokenizer.py, token_bucket.md, secret_sharing.rs are silently untracked, so code and config the operator expects committed never enters version control, with no error anywhere.
findings.required_change: Narrow the shipped patterns to the documented secret locations only (e.g. 'secrets/', '.env', '.env.*', '*.pem', plus at most '*secret*'/'*token*' anchored to a dedicated directory such as 'secrets/**' or '*.secret'), so legitimate source files whose names merely contain the substrings are not ignored; update SECRETS.md's C-12 wording if it names these patterns.

findings.evidence: The fixture seam swaps the real forge transport for attacker/operator-controlled data: "`preflight`, `apply`, and `verify` accept `--forge-fixture <file>`: the sanctioned fixture-backed seam that swaps the forge (gh) transport for a dataset-driven one" (ONBOARDING.md:173-175), while verify's output is committed truth: "`factory/PREFLIGHT.md` is regenerated on every run and is the **report of record**" (ONBOARDING.md:108) and the verify loop says "commit it" (ONBOARDING.md:154). The only guard separating a fixture-backed run from a real readiness record is prose — "a real onboarding session never passes it" (ONBOARDING.md:176) — nothing in the documented behavior marks, refuses, or distinguishes a PREFLIGHT.md produced under --forge-fixture. Mutation: run `verify --forge-fixture f.json` against a green fixture dataset and commit the resulting report of record; downstream consumers (KICKOFF cold start reads "factory/PREFLIGHT.md (the latest verify result)", ONBOARDING.md's kickoff message) accept it as real readiness.
findings.required_change: Make the fixture mode mechanically visible in the report of record: when verify runs with --forge-fixture, stamp the regenerated factory/PREFLIGHT.md with an unmissable fixture-mode marker (and record it in the onboarding/verify output), or refuse to write the report of record under a fixture unless an explicit override flag is passed, so a fixture-backed run can never produce an unmarked readiness record.

findings.evidence: The workflow changes deepen what untrusted-branch code can do without pinning token scope: the diff adds full-history checkout ('+          fetch-depth: 0   # full history — readiness pin-resolution checks', .github/workflows/kit-ci.yml:12) and a new step executing repo-controlled Python on every push/PR ('+      - name: Genericization tripwire (banned-token sweep)' / '+        run: python3 tools/check_genericization.py', lines 28-29). Neither hunk introduces or shows a least-privilege `permissions:` block, so the job's steps run with the repository's default GITHUB_TOKEN scope (write-all on private/legacy settings), wider than anything the listed steps need — a fork-branch or malicious-commit change to the executed scripts inherits that token.
findings.required_change: Add an explicit least-privilege permissions block to the workflow (e.g. `permissions: contents: read` at the workflow or job level) so the CI job's GITHUB_TOKEN is scoped to read-only regardless of repository defaults.

findings.evidence: The tripwire silently skips any file that is not valid UTF-8 or cannot be read: '+        except (UnicodeDecodeError, OSError):' / '+            continue  # binary/unreadable: skipped, never fatal' (tools/check_genericization.py:153-154). Mutation: append one invalid byte (e.g. 0xff) to a text file containing banned vocabulary and the file leaves the scan entirely — the gate stays green (exit 0, 'genericization: 0 hit(s)') while the leak ships, with no line naming the skipped file. The docstring makes the skip deliberate, but the skip is invisible in the output, so a bypass produces no signal.
findings.required_change: Make skips visible: print a one-line notice per skipped-but-git-tracked file (e.g. 'SKIP <path>: not valid UTF-8') and include the skip count in the summary, so a file silently dropping out of the tripwire's coverage is observable in CI logs; optionally fail when a text-extension file is undecodable.
